Global Markets Brief
Dear Investor,
This week, we look at a different side of market risk: liquidity. Turkey’s recent fund turmoil shows how strong returns can mask the difficulty of exiting crowded and illiquid positions when investors rush for the door. We examine how concentrated holdings, low free-float stocks, regulatory changes and redemption pressure turned a performance story into a liquidity crisis, and investors should look for beyond headline returns.

Equity · Emerging Market
Turkey's Funds' Alpha Backfired
How Turkey's Top Funds Ran Out of Room to Sell
On September 17, the regulator suspended purchases and redemptions in affected funds and ordered 130 funds managed by seven portfolio companies to be liquidated. The funds covered around 891 billion lira ($21.4bn) and roughly 353,000 investors. Several Turkish funds that had delivered exceptional returns suddenly struggled to meet investor withdrawals.
How The Returns Looked So Good
The story had been building for months. Some funds had built large positions in smaller companies with very low free float, meaning only a limited number of shares were available for public trading. As these stocks rose, the value of the funds' holdings and their NAVs also rose. Two Pusula funds gained 164% and 144% in the first seven months of 2026, attracting more investors and making the funds look increasingly successful.
The Problem Was In The Exit
The funds had become large holders of stocks that were difficult to sell in size. While prices were rising, this was not obvious because the funds could value their holdings at the market price. The problem appeared when investors wanted their money back. Funds needed cash, but selling large positions in thinly traded stocks could push prices lower, reducing NAV and making it harder to meet further withdrawals. Falling prices in these stocks made it difficult for funds to raise cash and forced some to sell other holdings as well.
The Rules Change Created More Problems
The warning had come earlier. On December 2, 2025, Turkey's Financial Stability Committee discussed unusual price movements in low-free-float stocks. The regulator then worked through several measures during 2026. TEFAS trading rules were approved on June 17 and implemented on July 20. On July 23, Turkey also changed the valuation of certain listed fund units, with the new treatment applying after July 31. The broader Investment Funds Guide was then updated on August 28, targeting risks linked to low-free-float shares, unusual price movements and fund structures.
Forced To Reduce Positions
The aim of the new rules was to reduce concentration and protect investors. But funds that had already built large positions now had to adjust them. That created a problem because these were the same stocks that were difficult to sell in large amounts. The regulation was addressing the concentration risk, but the process of reducing those positions added selling pressure to an already thin market.
September Turned It Into A Crisis
The pressure became visible on September 15, when Pusula reported problems meeting some withdrawal requests. On September 16, Tera reported similar difficulties and the BIST 100 fell more than 5%. By September 17, authorities had suspended the affected funds and ordered liquidations. The central bank increased repo funding to 300 billion lira, from 1 billion lira a day earlier, and raised banks' interbank borrowing limits tenfold.
Why It Matters
Strong returns alone do not tell investors how a fund will behave under stress. The Turkey episode shows why it is important to check what a fund owns, how concentrated it is, how much of those holdings can be traded and how quickly the fund may need to return cash to investors. A fund can look excellent during rising markets but become difficult to exit when many investors want their money back at the same time. The key lesson is simple: do not only ask how much a fund can make, also ask how easily you can get your money back.
